newsitem.title: USA: Jury selection begins slowly in Broin smoking case.
newsitem.headline: Jury selection begins slowly in Broin smoking case.

text.p: Jury selection in the Broin secondhand-smoke trial started slowly on Monday, with rival attorneys agreeing that a longtime smoker impatient with U.S. restrictions against cigarette use in public should not sit as a juror in the $5 billion case against tobacco companies.

Only six prospective jurors were questioned before a lunch break was called by Dade County Circuit Court Judge Robert Kaye. Another nine were to be questioned later Monday, with more than 200 others standing by for questioning by attorneys.

Six jurors and six to 12 alternates are needed for the trial of the landmark class-action lawsuit, filed on behalf of an estimated 60,000 non-smoking flight attendants with ailments allegedly caused by secondhand smoke on passenger flights. The trial is expected to last eight weeks or longer.
"It's going a lot slower than I thought it would," Kaye said.
Kaye released a second prospective juror, a south Florida attorney with a one-man law practice, because of potential hardship.

The judge refused a request by Susan Roseblatt, an attorney for the flight attendants, for the dismissal of two women in the pool of potential jurors. One of them said the ailing flight attendants should have found other work to avoid secondhand smoke, while the other wavered over whether she would be able to find the tobacco companies liable for the alleged injuries.
Lawyers on both sides are allowed refuse a limited number of potential jurors without explanation. Rosenblatt did not refuse either of the jurors but could do so later.

During the questioning, lawyers for both sides probed the potential jurors about their smoking habits and family medical histories connected to cigarettes. Jurors were also asked whether cigarettes and cigarette advertising should be banned in the United States.
The one juror both sides immediately agreed should be sent home described himself as a heavy smoker for decades and said, "I'm a smoker and my health is the same as it was when I started smoking."
